question: The honey produced by bees, especially organic honey, has natural antibacterial agents, enzymes, vitamins and minerals that protect our bodies from germs. It is a real health elixir. However, for various reasons, such as the use of pesticides, bees are either killed on the spot or some of their bodily functions are compromised, which results in humans being deprived of the invaluable product they produce.

This results in increased adulteration of honey, as it is blended with honey from outside the EU, mainly from China, Turkey and the United Kingdom. The consequence of this is that both producers who do not blend their honey and consumers who consume products of dubious quality and origin suffer. What steps is the Commission taking to protect producers who do not blend the honey they produce?
answer: Blending honeys of different geographical and/or botanical origins is standard practice. What matters is that all honey placed on the EU market, obtained in a single or in multiple country(ies) of origin, must comply with the requirements of the EU Honey Directive (1).

As the Commission set out in its replies to written questions E-000209/2024 (2) and 000343/2024 (3), a series of measures to address honey adulteration has already been taken at EU level, including reinforcement of import requirements for honey, launching a project aimed at harmonisation of analysis methods to detect new types of sugar-based adulterants used in honey, and reviewing the EU Honey Directive to increase honey traceability along the supply chain (4).
